To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the addition of vitamin D3 and Ca to a low Ca, low P diet improved bone ash and toe ash in ducklings.
the response of ducklings to dietary Ca and vitamin D3 was minimal, and that the response of the ducklings was not affected by phytase activity or intestinal vesicle calcium concentrations.
the response of BW gain, feed intake, toe ash, and P retention to increasing concentrations of dietary Ca was not linear but was quadratic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of dietary Ca and vitamin D3 concentrations on the performance and bone mineralization of Pekin ducks.
the effects of Ca and vitamin D3 supplementation on performance and skeletal development in Pekin drake ducklings.
the interaction of Ca and phytate-P in the diets of ducklings and the effect of dietary Ca on intestinal phytase and brush border vesicles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Ca requirement of Pekin drake ducklings is 0.85 to 0.95%.
the Ca concentration in the duckling diet should be maintained at 0.85%.
Ca concentrations of 0.95 or 0.85%, depending on the performance characteristic, are optimal for the growth of Pekin ducklings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dietary Ca concentration does not affect phytase activity or Ca transport in the small intestinal mucosa.
increasing dietary concentrations of Ca may decrease phytin-phosphorus hydro-lysis by chelation with Ca.
increasing dietary Ca did not negatively impact phytase activity or brush border vesicle phytase activity in the intestinal mucosa of Pekin ducks.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the dietary calcium concentration in the diet did not affect the kinetics of phytase activity, but it may affect the hydrolysis of phytate by binding to phytate and decreasing the availability of the phosphorus in the diet.
the dietary Ca requirement for ducks is lower than that for chickens.
increasing dietary Ca concentrations from 0.6 to 1.2 % did not affect P absorption and retention in ducks.
